facts.fact: Garra panitvongi was described as a new species in 2023 in the journal Zootaxa.
Its authors were Weerapongse Tangjitjaroen, Zachary Randall, Sampan Tongnunui, David Boyd and Larry Page.
It belongs to the genus Garra, in the subfamily Labeoninae of the family Cyprinidae.
It is the sixth Garra species known from the Salween River basin.
The name honours Dr. Nonn Panitvong for his contributions to the knowledge of Thai fishes, including his photographic guide to Thai freshwater fishes.
The holotype measures 67.8 mm SL and was collected in the Kasat River in Kanchanaburi Province, Thailand.
Its red-orange caudal fin and rear quarter of the body set it apart from all other Garra species.
It has a pointed proboscis marked with blue V-shaped stripes.
Unlike G. notata and G. salweenica, it lacks conspicuous black spots at the dorsal-fin base and large black spots or bands on the caudal fin.
It has 14–15 pectoral-fin rays, compared with 17–18 in G. salweenica.
The front of the body is olive-green and changes abruptly to bright orange and red towards the tail.
Its elongated snout is covered in tubercles that it can raise or lower.
It has a disc-shaped organ on the lower lip that works like a suction cup to grip rocks in the current.
The video says the front of the body can be grey, or sometimes blue or green, and suggests this may be linked to spawning.
It has not been evaluated for the IUCN Red List.
The video stresses that, although garras are often thought of as loach-like, they are cyprinids related to barbs and danios.
It is known from the Ataran River drainage in the Salween River basin, in southeastern Myanmar and western Thailand.
Specimens were collected in Kayin State in Myanmar and in the Kasat River in Kanchanaburi Province, Thailand.
Larry Page said it lives only in the Ataran River basin; the Kasat River, where it was collected, is a tributary of the Ataran.
The species is known only from a small stretch of the Kasat River on the Thailand–Myanmar border.
Specimens were collected in swift, rocky riffles.
It lives in shallow, fast-flowing, clear streams and rivers, where it is easy to see on the bottom.
Its habitat is isolated and hard to reach.
It has been sold in the aquarium trade since at least the early 2000s, long before it was formally described.
Nonn Panitvong and a friend found a population in 2006 and helped introduce the fish to the trade.
The video says the species is uncommon in the hobby but is becoming more mainstream and is not expensive.
Because its range is so restricted, the researchers' early assumption that it was widespread in Myanmar turned out to be wrong.
The video's keeper houses six of them in a 40-gallon breeder tank with large rocks, driftwood and big plants, giving each fish its own territory.
For breeding, the video suggests a long tank such as a 33-gallon long.
The video calls it forgiving on water parameters: upper 60s to low 80s °F and pH 6 to 7.5.
According to the video, it needs very clean, highly oxygenated water with strong flow, and it likes to sit in the current from the filter.
The video recommends a sandy or river-rock substrate, with rocks, driftwood and plants to break lines of sight.
In the wild it mainly eats algae and sometimes arthropods, which it scrapes off rocks with specialised mouthparts.
The video describes it as an omnivore that leans heavily towards plant food and grazes algae all day.
The video's keeper adds frozen worms, frozen brine shrimp or freeze-dried meaty foods once or twice a week.
Its tubercles seem to be used as weapons, based on aggressive behaviour seen in aquaria.
The video says it is feistier than other garras and each fish needs its own territory, but they do not seriously hurt each other.
According to the video, it spars only with other garras, not with corydoras, loaches or dwarf cichlids.
The tubercles may help attract mates or deter rivals.
The video says females can become somewhat chunkier than the slender males.
In aquaria, the video says there are few breeding reports; some people have spawned it, but methods are not documented.
The video describes it as a seasonal egg-scattering spawner and suggests a long tank with a rock pile and powerheads so the current carries eggs into the rocks.
